tagline: Probably the earliest of Paul's surviving letters, written to a young and persecuted church to encourage it, instruct it in holiness, and comfort it about believers who had died.
overview:
First Thessalonians is very likely the oldest surviving letter of Paul, and so one of the oldest documents in the New Testament, written around AD 50, about twenty years after the death and resurrection of Jesus. Paul, with Silvanus and Timothy, writes to a church he had founded only months before in Thessalonica, the leading city of Macedonia. He had been forced to leave suddenly, the new believers faced hostility from their neighbors, and he had no way of knowing whether their faith had survived. When Timothy returned with good news, Paul wrote this letter of relief, thanks, and encouragement.

The first three chapters are personal. Paul thanks God that the Thessalonians turned to God from idols, recalls how he and his companions lived among them like a nursing mother and a father, defends the sincerity of their conduct, and explains how desperately he wanted to see them again. The last two chapters give instruction: live in holiness and sexual purity, love one another, work quietly with your own hands, and do not grieve over believers who have died as if you had no hope, because the Lord will come and the dead in Christ will rise. The Day of the Lord will come like a thief, so stay awake and sober, and live together as a church in peace, joy, prayer, and thanks.

The letter shows the Christian faith in its earliest written form, and it already contains the heart of it: God the Father, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit; Jesus' death and resurrection; turning from idols to the living God; and waiting for his Son from heaven. Its triad of faith, love, and hope (1:3; 5:8) sets the tone for everything after.
author: Paul wrote 1 Thessalonians, with Silvanus (the Silas of Acts) and Timothy named alongside him (1:1). Its authenticity is accepted by nearly all scholars. The letter's warmth, its detailed memories of the founding visit, and its fit with the account in Acts 17 all point to Paul, and it was included in the earliest collections of his letters. Although three names stand in the greeting and the letter often says we, Paul speaks in the first person at key moments (2:18; 3:5; 5:27), which shows him as its principal author.
date: Paul wrote from Corinth, shortly after Timothy rejoined him there (3:6; compare Acts 18:5). Paul's stay in Corinth can be dated fairly closely because Acts 18:12 places the proconsul Gallio there during it, and an inscription found at Delphi dates Gallio's term in Achaia to about AD 51 to 52. That places the letter around AD 50 or 51, making it very likely Paul's earliest surviving letter. The one serious rival is Galatians, which some scholars date around AD 48 on the view that it was written to churches in southern Galatia before the Jerusalem council of Acts 15; most who date Galatians later regard 1 Thessalonians as the earliest.
setting:
Thessalonica was founded around 316 BC by Cassander, one of the successors of Alexander the Great, who named it after his wife Thessalonike, Alexander's half-sister. It had a fine harbor on the Thermaic Gulf and stood on the Via Egnatia, the great Roman road that crossed the Balkans, so trade, travelers, and news passed through it constantly. When Rome organized Macedonia as a province in the 140s BC, Thessalonica became its capital. Because it sided with Antony and Octavian in the civil war of 42 BC, it was rewarded as a free city, governed by its own magistrates, whom Acts calls politarchs (Acts 17:6), a title confirmed by inscriptions from the city. The city honored Rome and its emperors, and it was home to many cults, including Egyptian gods, Dionysus, and the local cult of Cabirus, as well as a Jewish synagogue.

Acts 17:1-10 tells the story of the church's founding on Paul's second missionary trip, around AD 49 or 50, after he and Silas had been beaten and jailed in Philippi (compare 1 Thessalonians 2:2). For three Sabbaths Paul reasoned in the synagogue from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise, and some Jews, a large number of God-fearing Greeks, and a number of leading women believed. Opposition then stirred up a mob, which dragged Jason, Paul's host, before the city officials and accused the missionaries of defying Caesar's decrees by saying there is another king, Jesus. Paul and Silas were sent away by night to Berea and then Paul went on to Athens and Corinth. The letter itself suggests the church was largely Gentile, since its members had turned to God from idols (1:9), and that Paul had stayed long enough to work at his trade and to receive gifts from Philippi more than once (2:9; Philippians 4:16).
purpose: Paul writes, first, out of relief and love: to thank God for the church's faith under pressure and to renew the bond that had been broken by his sudden departure (2:17 to 3:10). Second, he defends his own conduct, apparently against suggestions that he had been one more traveling speaker out for money or praise who abandoned his followers (2:1-12). Third, he gives instruction the young church needed: on sexual holiness in a culture with very different standards, on brotherly love and daily work, on the fate of believers who had died before the Lord's coming, on readiness for the Day of the Lord, and on the life of the congregation (chapters 4 and 5).
story: First Thessalonians fills out the brief account of Acts 17 and shows what happened after Paul left a city. It stands at the point where the gospel had just crossed from Asia into Europe, through Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, Athens, and Corinth. In the larger story of the Bible it shows Gentiles turning from idols to the living God, as the prophets had said the nations would, and it looks forward to the coming of the Lord, the Day of the Lord announced by the prophets from Amos onward, now understood as the return of Jesus. Second Thessalonians follows closely and continues the same conversation.
christ: Even in this early letter, Jesus is spoken of in the same breath as God the Father as the source of grace and peace (1:1) and as the one who, with the Father, can direct Paul's way (3:11). He is God's Son, raised from the dead, who rescues believers from the coming wrath (1:10). He died for us so that we may live together with him (5:10). His coming, the parousia, is the horizon of the whole letter (2:19; 3:13; 4:15; 5:23). Believers who have died are the dead in Christ, and the end of the story is that we will always be with the Lord (4:16-17).
reading: Read 1 Thessalonians as a pastor's letter to new converts, full of emotion and memory as well as instruction. Watch for the repeated you know, as Paul reminds the church of what they already experienced and were taught, and for the triad of faith, love, and hope. Notice how often teaching about the Lord's coming is tied to comfort and to conduct rather than to calculation. The passage on the dead in Christ (4:13-18) is central to later debates about the rapture and the order of end-time events; read it first for what Paul says it is for, that believers may encourage one another and not grieve as those without hope, before asking how it fits a larger scheme.

structure.title: Thanksgiving for the church
structure.summary: Paul thanks God for the Thessalonians' faith, love, and hope, and for how they welcomed the gospel and turned from idols to serve the living God.

structure.title: Paul's conduct among them
structure.summary: Paul recalls how he and his companions preached with integrity, lived gently among them, and worked night and day, and thanks God that they received the word of God.

structure.title: Paul's longing and Timothy's report
structure.summary: Kept away by force, Paul sent Timothy to strengthen them; Timothy's good news brings him joy, and he prays to see them and for their love to grow.

structure.title: Living to please God
structure.summary: Instruction on sexual holiness, brotherly love, and a quiet life of work that earns the respect of outsiders.

structure.title: The Lord's coming
structure.summary: The dead in Christ will rise and all believers will be with the Lord; the Day of the Lord will come like a thief, so live as children of the day.

structure.title: Life together and farewell
structure.summary: Respect leaders, care for one another, rejoice, pray, give thanks, test prophecy, and receive a closing blessing.

themes.title: Faith, love, and hope
themes.body: Paul thanks God for the church's work of faith, labor of love, and enduring hope (1:3), and later describes faith and love as a breastplate and the hope of salvation as a helmet (5:8). The three words, which appear together again in 1 Corinthians 13:13, summarize the Christian life as trust in God, love for others, and confident waiting for Christ.

themes.title: The coming of the Lord
themes.body: Every chapter closes on or near a reference to the Lord's return. Paul uses the word parousia, the term for a ruler's arrival or official visit, and he speaks of it as the believers' hope, the time when their faithfulness will be revealed, and the reunion of the living with those who have died. It is also the Day of the Lord, which will come suddenly on those who are not ready.

themes.title: Suffering and endurance
themes.body: The church received the word in much affliction (1:6), and Paul reminds them that he warned them trials would come (3:3-4). Their perseverance under pressure is evidence of God's work. The letter does not explain suffering away; it sets it within the pattern of Jesus, the prophets, and the churches in Judea, and within the hope of his coming.

themes.title: Holiness
themes.body: God's will is the church's sanctification (4:3). Holiness in this letter is practical: sexual purity, honesty in dealings, love, and hard work, and it is also God's own work, since Paul prays that the God of peace will sanctify them completely (5:23). The Spirit given to them is called holy (4:8).

themes.title: A pastor's love
themes.body: No letter of Paul shows more openly the affection between a missionary and a young church. He compares himself to a nursing mother and a father, speaks of being orphaned when separated from them, and says he can go on living now that he knows they stand firm. The letter models ministry as shared life, not only shared message (2:8).

keyChapters.why: A compact picture of conversion in the first generation: the gospel coming in power and the Spirit, and Gentiles turning from idols to serve God and await his Son.
Paul's account of how he and his companions conducted themselves, one of the fullest pictures of his ministry and motives in any of his letters.
Instruction on holiness and daily work, and the passage on believers who have died and the Lord's coming (4:13-18).
The Day of the Lord coming like a thief, and a series of brief commands for church life, including rejoice, pray without ceasing, and give thanks.
